1. My First Home

6. Worn Down
7. Home at Last

Black Beauty was written by Anna Sewell and first published in 1877. Told in the voice of the horse himself, it was written to teach people to treat animals with kindness. The book was so powerful that it actually changed how horses were treated, and helped end some of the cruel practices it described. It remains one of the best-loved animal stories ever written.

My story is told by me, a horse, for this is my own life as I lived it. When I was young, I was called Black Beauty, for I was a fine black horse with one white foot and a white star upon my forehead. My first home was a pleasant green meadow with a clear pond, where I lived happily beside my gentle mother.

image.note: A young black foal with a white star grazing beside its mother in a lush green meadow by a pond; peaceful, warm

pages.text: My mother was wise, and she gave me advice I never forgot. She told me to be gentle and good, to do my work with a willing heart, and never to bite or kick, whatever happened. Good horses, she said, come from good ways, not just good blood. I tried all my life to live by her kind words, through easy days and very hard ones alike.

image.note: The mother horse standing tenderly over her foal, as if teaching it; a bond of love and wisdom

pages.text: When I grew big enough, I had to be broken in, that is, trained to wear a saddle and bridle and to pull a carriage. It was strange and a little frightening to have iron in my mouth and a weight on my back. But my first master was patient and kind, and he trained me gently, never with cruelty. A horse trained with kindness, I learned, serves with a glad and willing heart.

image.note: A patient trainer gently fitting a young horse with its first bridle and saddle; calm, trusting; kindness

pages.text: I was sold to a fine house with a good and gentle master, and there I was happy. I made a dear friend, a spirited mare named Ginger, who had once been treated cruelly and so was wary and quick to anger. Through kindness, Ginger slowly grew calmer and more trusting. I saw then how much of a creature's temper depends on how it has been treated.

image.note: Black Beauty beside a chestnut mare, Ginger, in a comfortable stable; two horse friends; the mare wary at first

pages.text: My good master and his kind groom cared for us wonderfully. One stormy night, I carried my master on an urgent errand across a flooded river in the dark. When we reached a bridge, I stopped dead and would not cross, no matter how he urged me, for I sensed something was wrong. It turned out the bridge had been broken by the flood. My caution had saved us both.

image.note: A horse refusing to cross a dark, broken bridge in a storm; the rider realising the danger; loyalty, instinct

pages.text: Those were the happiest years of my life. I was well fed, well groomed, and never worked beyond my strength. My master understood horses and treated us as friends, not machines. If all masters were like him, I thought, no horse in the world would ever suffer. But such kindness, I would sadly learn, was not to be my fortune forever.

image.note: Black Beauty content and gleaming in a sunny paddock with his kind master nearby; a golden, happy time

pages.text: Sadly, my kind mistress fell ill and had to move far away, so all the horses were sold. I was passed to a grand new household, where a cruel fashion caused me much suffering. The fine lady insisted our heads be strapped up high and tight by a cruel harness called a bearing rein, purely for show, though it hurt us and made our work far harder.

image.note: A horse forced into a tight, high-strapped harness for fashion, its neck arched painfully; vain cruelty; the horse enduring

pages.text: My poor friend Ginger, with her spirited temper, could not bear such treatment as I could, and it broke her health and her heart. After that, I was sold on again and again, each master a little less careful than the last. Slowly I passed from a life of comfort down into a life of hard, weary labour. A horse, I found, is only as safe as its master is kind.

image.note: A weary horse being led from a fine stable to a plainer one; the descent into harder times; sombre but gentle

pages.text: At last I was sold to pull a cab in the great, noisy city. My master there was a good, honest, poor man named Jerry, who was kind to me even though he had little himself. We worked long hours on hard stone streets, in all weathers, but Jerry never once beat me or worked me cruelly, and for that I was deeply grateful. Kindness, even in hardship, means everything to a horse.

image.note: Black Beauty pulling a cab through a busy old city street; a kind, poor cabman, Jerry, at the reins; hard but humane

pages.text: The city was hard on horses. I saw many worked far past their strength by uncaring owners, and it grieved me. But good Jerry cared for me well, and his cheerful family loved me. For a while, even in that difficult place, I had a home and a master who valued me. Sadly, poor Jerry fell gravely ill and could work no more, and once again I had to be sold.

image.note: Jerry's warm family patting the horse; then Jerry ill and the horse sold again; a bittersweet parting

pages.text: Now came the hardest days of all. I fell into the hands of harsh owners who worked me mercilessly, gave me too little food, and cared nothing for my suffering. I had once been the handsome, happy Black Beauty of a fine green meadow. Now I was thin, tired and worn, pulling heavy loads with aching legs. I began to fear I would be worked until I simply dropped.

image.note: A thin, weary, aging horse straining under a heavy load, its coat dull; the low point; sad but never graphic

pages.text: One dreadful day, overloaded and exhausted, I stumbled and fell in the street, and could not rise. I lay there, worn out and hopeless, and thought my life was surely ending. But even then, a kind stranger stopped and insisted I be cared for and rested, rather than driven on. A single act of kindness, once more, gave me back my life.

image.note: The fallen horse in the street; a kind passer-by stopping to help and insisting it be rested; compassion; hopeful turn

pages.text: When I had rested and grown a little stronger, I was taken to a sale, and there, by the greatest good fortune, I was bought by kind ladies with a gentle groom, a groom who, wonderfully, recognised me as the fine horse I had once been in my happy youth. They took me to a peaceful country home to live out my days in comfort and rest.

image.note: The horse recognised and lovingly bought by kind new owners; led toward a green, peaceful country home; joy, relief

pages.text: And so, after all my wandering and hardship, I came home at last to green meadows very like the ones where I was born. I am old now, and my hard days are behind me, and I am loved and well cared for. My mother's words held true through it all: I did my work with a willing heart, and in the end, kindness found me again.

image.note: The old horse grazing peacefully in a sunny green meadow at last, contented; a gentle, happy ending; closing
